entries: What are the laws of thermodynamics?

The laws of thermodynamics:
- Zeroth: if A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, they're in equilibrium with each other (this defines temperature).
- First: energy is conserved: ΔU = Q − W.
- Second: the entropy of an isolated system never decreases, so heat flows from hot to cold by itself.
- Third: entropy approaches a minimum as temperature approaches absolute zero, which can't be reached.
Entropy is a measure of disorder, or of the number of ways a system can be arranged. In an isolated system it never decreases (second law of thermodynamics).

Quantum mechanics is the physics of very small things (atoms, electrons, photons). Energy comes in packets (quanta), particles behave like waves, and outcomes are probabilities. Pioneers: Planck, Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Schrödinger.
What is the Heisenberg uncertainty principle?
The uncertainty principle: you can't know both the position and the momentum of a particle exactly at the same time: Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π.
Wave–particle duality: light and matter behave both as waves and as particles. de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p links a particle's momentum to its wavelength.
The photoelectric effect: light shining on a metal ejects electrons, but only if its frequency is above a threshold. Einstein explained it with photons (E = hf) and won the 1921 Nobel Prize for it.
What are special and general relativity?
Einstein's special relativity (1905): the speed of light is the same for everyone, so moving clocks run slow and E = mc². General relativity (1915): gravity is the curving of space-time by mass.

The Doppler effect: the pitch (frequency) of a wave rises when the source comes towards you and falls when it moves away, like a passing ambulance siren. Redshift of galaxies is the same effect for light.
The electromagnetic spectrum, from longest to shortest wavelength: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.
Total internal reflection happens when light in a denser medium hits the boundary at more than the critical angle, and all of it reflects back. Optical fibres and diamonds' sparkle use it.
Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v − 1/u, magnification m = v/u. Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, m = −v/u (New Cartesian sign convention). Power of a lens P = 1/f (f in metres), in dioptres.
Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its colours (VIBGYOR) by a prism, because each colour bends by a different amount. Violet bends most, red least.

A semiconductor, like silicon or germanium, conducts electricity between a conductor and an insulator. Adding impurities (doping) makes n-type (extra electrons) or p-type (holes). Chips, diodes and transistors are made from them.
A diode lets current flow in only one direction. It's made of a p–n junction and is used to convert AC to DC (rectification). LEDs are diodes that give out light.
A transistor is a semiconductor device that switches or amplifies electric signals. Billions of them in a chip do a computer's calculations.
What is the difference between AC and DC?
DC (direct current) flows one way, as from a battery. AC (alternating current) keeps reversing direction: Indian mains is 220–230 V AC at 50 Hz.
A transformer changes AC voltage using electromagnetic induction between two coils: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. Step-up transformers raise voltage; step-down ones lower it.

An electric motor turns electrical energy into motion: a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field feels a force (Fleming's left-hand rule) and spins. A generator does the reverse (Fleming's right-hand rule).
Coulomb's law: the force between two charges is F = kq₁q₂/r², with k ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
A capacitor stores electric charge and energy between two plates: Q = CV, energy = ½CV². Capacitance is measured in farads (F).
Kirchhoff's current law: the total current into a junction equals the total current out. Kirchhoff's voltage law: the voltages around any closed loop add to zero.
Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to escape a planet's gravity without further push: v = √(2GM/R). For Earth it's about 11.2 km/s.

Kepler's laws of planetary motion: 1) planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus; 2) a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times; 3) T² ∝ r³ (period squared is proportional to the orbit size cubed).
Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is back-and-forth motion where the restoring force is proportional to displacement (F = −kx), like a pendulum or a spring. Its period is T = 2π√(m/k).
Bernoulli's principle: where a fluid flows faster, its pressure is lower. It helps explain how aeroplane wings get lift.
Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is passed equally in all directions. Hydraulic lifts and brakes work this way.
Surface tension is the 'skin' on a liquid's surface caused by molecules pulling on each other. It lets insects walk on water and makes drops round.
Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flowing: honey is more viscous than water.

Gas laws: Boyle's law PV = constant (fixed temperature); Charles's law V/T = constant (fixed pressure); Gay-Lussac's law P/T = constant; Avogadro's law V ∝ n. Together: ideal gas law PV = nRT, with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).

Radioactivity is the spontaneous breakdown of unstable nuclei, giving out alpha particles (helium nuclei, stopped by paper), beta particles (electrons, stopped by aluminium) or gamma rays (electromagnetic, need thick lead).
Half-life is the time for half of a radioactive sample to decay. After n half-lives, (½)ⁿ of it remains. Carbon-14's half-life is about 5,730 years, which is used for carbon dating.
Superconductivity is when some materials, cooled below a critical temperature, conduct electricity with zero resistance and push out magnetic fields. It's used in MRI machines.

Across a period (left to right): atomic size decreases; ionisation energy and electronegativity increase. Down a group: atomic size increases; ionisation energy and electronegativity decrease. Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
What are the types of chemical reactions?

Main types: combination (A + B → AB), decomposition (AB → A + B), displacement (A + BC → AC + B), double displacement (AB + CD → AD + CB), redox (oxidation and reduction together), and combustion (burning in oxygen).
What are the types of chemical bonds?
Chemical bonds: ionic (electrons transferred, e.g. NaCl), covalent (electrons shared, e.g. H₂O), metallic (a sea of electrons in metals), and the weaker hydrogen bonds between molecules.
A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F and another electronegative atom. It gives water its high boiling point and holds DNA's two strands together.
Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls shared electrons towards itself. Fluorine is the highest (4.0 on the Pauling scale).

One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number). The mass of one mole in grams equals the molar mass. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass. At STP, one mole of gas fills 22.4 L. Try: "number of moles in 36 g of water".
Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds. Hydrocarbons: alkanes (single bonds, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, e.g. methane), alkenes (a double bond, CₙH₂ₙ, e.g. ethene), alkynes (a triple bond, CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, e.g. ethyne).
Functional groups decide how organic compounds react: alcohol (−OH), aldehyde (−CHO), ketone (>C=O), carboxylic acid (−COOH), ester (−COO−), amine (−NH₂), halo (−Cl, −Br).
Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures, e.g. butane and isobutane (both C₄H₁₀).
A polymer is a very long molecule made of repeating units (monomers). Examples: polythene, PVC, nylon, rubber, proteins, DNA and starch.
Electrolysis uses electricity to drive a chemical change, e.g. splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen, or electroplating. Positive ions go to the cathode (−) and negative ions to the anode (+).
Oxidation is losing electrons (or gaining oxygen); reduction is gaining electrons (or losing oxygen). Remember OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. They always happen together (redox).
Le Chatelier's principle: if you change the conditions of a reaction at equilibrium (concentration, pressure, temperature), the equilibrium shifts to reduce that change.
Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react. A catalyst lowers it, speeding the reaction without being used up.
An exothermic reaction gives out heat (like burning or respiration). An endothermic reaction takes in heat (like photosynthesis or dissolving ammonium chloride).
What is the difference between mitosis and meiosis?
Mitosis makes 2 identical cells with the full set of chromosomes (for growth and repair). Meiosis makes 4 cells with half the chromosomes (gametes: sperm and egg), each genetically different.
What is the central dogma of biology?
The central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein. DNA is copied (replication), transcribed into messenger RNA (transcription), and RNA is translated into protein at ribosomes (translation).

Mendel's laws of inheritance: the law of dominance (one allele can hide another), the law of segregation (the two alleles separate into different gametes), and the law of independent assortment (different traits are inherited independently).
What is the difference between genotype and phenotype?

Genotype is the set of genes an organism carries (like Tt); phenotype is the trait you can see (like tall). A dominant allele (T) shows even with one copy; a recessive one (t) shows only with two copies.
The nitrogen cycle: bacteria fix nitrogen from the air into the soil (nitrogen fixation), plants take it up, animals eat plants, and decomposers and denitrifying bacteria return it to the air.
The carbon cycle: plants take in CO₂ for photosynthesis; animals eat plants; respiration, decay and burning fuels return CO₂ to the air.

The circulatory system: the heart pumps blood through arteries (away from the heart), capillaries (exchange with cells) and veins (back to the heart). Red blood cells carry oxygen, white blood cells fight infection, platelets help clotting.
The endocrine system uses hormones: pituitary (the master gland), thyroid (thyroxine), pancreas (insulin controls blood sugar), adrenal (adrenaline), and the ovaries and testes (sex hormones).
Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living things without being used up, e.g. amylase breaks starch into sugar and pepsin breaks down protein.
The immune system defends the body. White blood cells attack germs; antibodies lock onto specific invaders; vaccines train the immune system in advance using a harmless piece or version of a germ.
What is the difference between a virus and bacteria?

Bacteria are living single cells that can reproduce by themselves; many are helpful, and antibiotics treat bacterial infections. Viruses are much smaller, can only reproduce inside a host cell, and aren't killed by antibiotics.
ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy currency of the cell: breaking its phosphate bond releases energy for muscles, nerves and making molecules.
Homeostasis is how the body keeps its inside conditions steady, like temperature (about 37 °C), blood sugar and water balance, using feedback.
